wrong_text: roughly 820 million people do not have enough to eat
problem: The 820 million figure is the ~2019/2020 FAO estimate, now significantly outdated. The FAO State of Food Security report 2024 gives 733 million undernourished (2023 midpoint estimate) and 673 million for 2024. Presenting 820 million as a current figure overstates hunger by ~90–150 million people. Source: FAO 'The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2024'.
correction: roughly 733 million people do not have enough to eat

wrong_text: Around 820 million people worldwide are chronically undernourished.
problem: Same outdated figure repeated in the Key Fact box. FAO 2024 report gives 733 million (2023 data) as the current midpoint estimate. The 820M figure dates from around 2019–2020.
correction: Around 733 million people worldwide are chronically undernourished.

problem: The MCQ option and correct answer key reference the outdated 820 million figure. Should be updated to match the corrected 733 million figure so the quiz answer is accurate.

wrong_text: draws water from the Indus River and its tributaries (the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej)
problem: Under the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, the Beas is one of the three Eastern Rivers allocated to India, not Pakistan. Pakistan's share of the rivers is the Indus, Jhelum and Chenab (Western Rivers). The Ravi and Sutlej were also Eastern Rivers given to India (Pakistan retains only limited existing uses from them). Listing Beas as a river the IBIS draws from is factually incorrect and contradicts the same lesson's paragraph on the Indus Waters Treaty. Source: World Bank Fact Sheet on the Indus Waters Treaty 1960; Wikipedia Indus Waters Treaty.
correction: draws water from the Indus River and its tributaries (the Jhelum, Chenab and Ravi) through a system of three major dams (Tarbela, Mangla and Chashma), 19 barrages and over 58,000 km of canals

wrong_text: the NGO Excellent Development has built hundreds of sand dams since 1999
problem: Excellent Development (now Sand Dams Worldwide) was established in 2002, not 1999. Multiple sources including SSWM and the organisation's own documentation confirm the 2002 founding date. Sand dams in Kenya predate the NGO (Joshua Mukusya pioneered them from 1980), but Excellent Development as an organisation began in 2002. Source: SSWM 'Excellent Development — Sand Dams in Kenya'; Sand Dams Worldwide history.
correction: the NGO Excellent Development has built hundreds of sand dams since 2002

field: content_html (n30) — number of dams in Makueni
wrong_text: By 2023, Excellent Development had built over 800 sand dams in Makueni
problem: The '800+ dams in Makueni' figure conflates two separate facts. Excellent Development has enabled ~884 sand dams across rural Kenya as a whole (across multiple counties and countries), not 800+ in Makueni County specifically. Makueni County has over 1,000 sand dams in total, but these are built by multiple organisations. Excellent Development's own country-wide Kenya total is cited as 533–884 dams depending on the source year. Attributing 800+ to Makueni alone for a single NGO is an overstatement. The claim about 100,000 people served is plausible for the broader programme but the geographic scope needs qualifying.
correction: By 2023, Excellent Development had supported the building of over 800 sand dams across rural Kenya (including Makueni County), serving more than 100,000 people

wrong_text: An estimated 14 million hectares — around a quarter of all irrigated land — is affected by waterlogging or salinity
problem: The 14 million hectares figure cannot be verified from WAPDA or peer-reviewed sources and appears inflated. Current WAPDA estimates give waterlogging at 4.5–7.1 million hectares and salinity at 5.3–6.3 million hectares (separately). Even combined, these reach ~10–13 million hectares at the high end, and most authoritative sources cite lower figures. The '14 million hectares' is widely repeated in GCSE resources but originates from older, unverified estimates. The parenthetical 'around a quarter' is roughly consistent with 14M out of 18M ha but the base figure is questionable. Sources: WAPDA 2003 via ICARDA; envpk.com; Dialogue Earth.
correction: An estimated 6–10 million hectares of irrigated land is affected by waterlogging or salinity, cutting yields and in severe cases rendering land uncultivable

wrong_text: The UN estimates that around 24 billion tonnes of fertile soil are lost each year to erosion
problem: FAO's authoritative Status of the World's Soil Resources report gives the figure as 25–40 billion tonnes of topsoil eroded per year, not 24 billion. The 24 billion figure is slightly below the accepted FAO range. '25 billion tonnes' would be the defensible low-end FAO figure. Source: FAO Global Symposium on Soil Erosion key messages; FAO newsroom 2015.
correction: The UN estimates that around 25 billion tonnes of fertile soil are lost each year to erosion
